Title: A moment of maritime opportunity? The U.S. Navy operational energy challenge
Source title: Journal of Marine Engineering and Technology
Affiliations: Herren Associates, Inc., Washington, DC, United States; United States Department of the Navy, Washington, DC, United States; United States Navy (Ret.), Washington, DC, United States
Authors with affiliations: Voth J.M., Herren Associates, Inc., Washington, DC, United States; Pence E.G., United States Department of the Navy, Washington, DC, United States; Sorrentino V., United States Navy (Ret.), Washington, DC, United States; Sturtevant G.H., United States Department of the Navy, Washington, DC, United States
Abstract: The U.S. Department of Defense's National Defense Strategy prioritises the U.S. Navy's focus on strategic competitors, equipped with long-range weapons, significant anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) systems, and substantial cyber capabilities. This paper analyses the U.S. Navy's efforts to field an energy-resilient force able to support distributed operations in a globally contested logistics environment. Specifically, it examines operational energy strategies, focusing on energy supportability and demand reduction, against the backdrop of naval power and energy system developments. Moreover, it advocates for the application of updated performance metrics to spur technological innovation and policy formulation, advance a data-driven culture, and inform pathways to support a whole-of-government approach to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. © 2024 Institute of Marine Engineering, Science & Technology.

Title: When Does Competition Become Conflict? Technology, Geography, and the Offense-Defense Balance
Authors with affiliations: Blagden D., University of Exeter, United Kingdom
Abstract: Is there a meaningful offense-defense balance of technological, geographical, and human factors that substantially affects war likelihood and severity? Key contemporary policy debates are certainly infused with the notion, from the dangers of crisis instability in East Asia to the possible first-move advantages of cyber weaponry. Defensive realist theory, meanwhile, raises the possibility of inferring intent from external posture choices. Yet for offensive realists, such signaling is a doomed hope, because of aggressors' incentives to conceal their hostile intentions before turning extant military technology to offensive ends. This article suggests that both perspectives misstate the causal role of the offense-defense balance. Competition may be a general condition of international politics - but it only manifests itself as a military conflict, defined as "cold"or ultimately "hot"war, under certain conditions. Specifically, the feasibility of advancing political goals via aggression rests on prevailing military technology, taken in its geographical context - that is, offense-defense calculations. Via three sub-theoretical cases - the "stopping power of water,"conventional blitzkrieg, and nuclear counterforce innovation - the article shows that the offense-defense balance affects conflict likelihood and severity even within offensive realism, specifically by affecting deterrence prospects. But this does not mean, as defensive realism posits, that the distinguishability of defense dominance promises a route out of the security dilemma.  © 2021 The Author(s) (2021).

Title: Maritime power in the digital age: China’s naval modernization and cyber-strategic expansion
Affiliations: Manipal Institute of Social Sciences Humanities and Arts, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India
Authors with affiliations: Singh N.K., Manipal Institute of Social Sciences Humanities and Arts, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India; Jash A., Manipal Institute of Social Sciences Humanities and Arts, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India
Abstract: China’s accelerated modernization of the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) and its expansive maritime infrastructure development are intensifying regional and global security concerns over cyber aggression and coercion. By deliberately blurring the boundaries between near and far seas, Beijing, through its actions, such as building artificial islands, deploying underwater drones, and establishing the Digital Silk Road (DSR), leverages engineering marvels to extend its geopolitical and military influence. These activities are further bolstered through the smart port initiatives, seabed sensor networks, and advanced naval assets such as frigates and aircraft carriers, collectively enabling more robust power projection across critical maritime domains. This is integrated with undersea cables and tunnels, which facilitate China’s surveillance and cyberespionage capabilities. Taken together, these dynamics highlight the urgent need for critical scrutiny of China’s quest for maritime power, which increasingly conceals geopolitical ambitions beneath the guise of developmental cooperation. © 2026 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

Abstract: the article presents a proposal for a conceptual model of the Maritime Power System at a strategic level in Colombia, to identify its different elements, actions and interactions, understanding the complexity of the phenomenon and facilitating the protection and defense of this power in terms of decision-making and resource management. Three phases were established for the development of the model. The first sought to identify the actors and elements that are part of the maritime power system in Colombia. The second phase focused on characterizing the relationships and interactions that exist between the elements of maritime power. In the third phase, the conceptual model of the maritime power system in Colombia was developed using the ISO 19450 standard, under the OPM methodology and the OPCAT OPM software. Finally, the main characteristics of the model and its importance for the Colombian Navy are highlighted. © 2022, Associacao Iberica de Sistemas e Tecnologias de Informacao. All rights reserved.

Title: Cybersecurity of Power Electronic Converters in Maritime Systems: Threat Landscape, Modeling, and Resilient Mitigation Strategies
Source title: 2025 10th International Conference on Smart and Sustainable Technologies, SpliTech 2025
Affiliations: Tallinn University of Technology, Estonian Maritime Academy, Tallinn, Estonia
Authors with affiliations: Rahimpour S., Tallinn University of Technology, Estonian Maritime Academy, Tallinn, Estonia; Shahin M., Tallinn University of Technology, Estonian Maritime Academy, Tallinn, Estonia; Bauk S., Tallinn University of Technology, Estonian Maritime Academy, Tallinn, Estonia
Abstract: With the increasing electrification and automation of maritime vessels, power electronic converters have become the backbone of shipboard power systems, interfacing various onboard generation sources with propulsion loads and auxiliary systems. These converters, integrated into a cyber-physical environment, are responsible for functions such as voltage and frequency control, reactive power compensation, and system stability support under dynamic maritime conditions. However, their increasing reliance on real-time data exchange, remote monitoring, and software-defined functionalities has led to a significant rise in cybersecurity exposure. The growing attack surface, exacerbated by communication interfaces and over-the-air firmware updates, makes shipboard power converters a critical vulnerability point in maritime operations. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of emerging cyber threats against power electronic converters in maritime environments, assessing current defense strategies and practical attack vectors. Furthermore, it proposes a structured security and resilience framework specifically tailored to shipboard converters, aiming to guide the design of cyber-resilient converter architectures and bridge the gap between cybersecurity and maritime power electronics domains.  © 2025 University of Split, FESB.

Abstract: The study of Japanese politics has flourished over the past several decades. This Handbook provides a state-of-the-field overview for students and researchers of Japanese. The volume also serves to introduce Japanese politics to readers less familiar with Japan. In addition, the volume has a theme of “evaluating Japan’s democracy.” Taken as a whole, the volume provides a positive evaluation of the state of Japan’s democracy. The volume is divided into two parts, roughly corresponding to domestic Japanese politics and Japan’s international politics. Title: A Privacy-Preserving Decentralized Optimization Framework for Generator Fuel Costs in Multi-Microgrid Networks
Source title: 2026 IEEE Texas Power and Energy Conference, TPEC 2026
Affiliations: Naval Surface Warfare Center Philadelphia, Department of the Navy, Philadelphia, PA, United States; Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, United States
Authors with affiliations: Amato J., Naval Surface Warfare Center Philadelphia, Department of the Navy, Philadelphia, PA, United States; Bose A., Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, United States; Bai L., Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, United States
Abstract: This paper presents a distributed optimization framework for fuel-efficient power dispatch in microgrids, applied to a marine electric propulsion system. The approach integrates multivariable fuel models with a modified consensus based Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) formulation that enables each generator to independently optimize its operating point while satisfying global power balance constraints. The framework maintains a level of data privacy between units, reducing communication overhead and minimizing vulnerabilities to cyber attacks. The method accommodates realistic nonlinear specific fuel consumption (SFC) maps for variable speed generators as well as energy storage (ES) devices whose power and state-of-charge dynamics are optimized as part of the ADMM algorithm. The resulting optimization coordinates generator outputs and ES schedules across a prediction horizon without requiring raw data sharing between units. Simulation results demonstrate that the distributed ADMM approach achieves dispatch solutions identical to a centralized benchmark while reducing communication requirements and computational burden. The method exhibits reliable convergence for systems with up to several dozen generators and effectively leverages storage to smooth rapid load fluctuations and reduce total fuel consumption. These results show that distributed ADMM provides a scalable, privacy-preserving alternative to centralized economic dispatch for next-generation microgrids and maritime power systems.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Chinese foreign policy: An introduction, fourth edition
Source title: Chinese Foreign Policy: An Introduction, Fourth Edition
Authors with affiliations: Lanteigne M., University of Tromsø, Norway
Abstract: This updated and expanded fourth edition of Chinese Foreign Policy seeks to examine the decision-makers, processes, and rationales behind China’s expanding international relations as well as offering an in-depth look at China’s modern global relations. Among the key issues explored in this edition are: The further expansion of Chinese foreign policy from regional (Asia-Pacific) to international interests; How the government of Xi Jinping has pursued a more confident great power foreign policy agenda; China’s growing economic power in an era of global financial uncertainty and the return of protectionism; Modern security challenges, including counter-terrorism, cyber-security, maritime power, military reform and modernisation, and the protection of overseas economic interests; China’s shifting power relationship with the United States under President Donald Trump; The deeper engagement of Beijing with a growing number of international and regional institutions and legal affairs; Cross-regional diplomacy, including updated sections on Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Russia/Eurasia, as well as Oceania and the Polar regions; The development of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) as a centrepiece of China’s foreign policy.This book will be essential reading for students of Chinese foreign policy and Asian international relations (IR), and is highly recommended for students of diplomacy, international security, and IR in general. © 2020 Marc Lanteigne. Abstract: The study of Japanese politics has flourished over the past several decades. This Handbook provides a state-of-the-field overview for students and researchers of Japanese. The volume also serves to introduce Japanese politics to readers less familiar with Japan. In addition, the volume has a theme of “evaluating Japan’s democracy.” Taken as a whole, the volume provides a positive evaluation of the state of Japan’s democracy. The volume is divided into two parts, roughly corresponding to domestic Japanese politics and Japan’s international politics. Within the domestic politics part, there are four distinct sections: “Domestic Political Actors and Institutions, " covering the Japanese Constitution, electoral systems, prime minister, Diet, bureaucracy, judiciary, and local government; “Political Parties and Coalitions, " covering the Liberal Democratic Party, coalition government, Kōmeitō, and the political opposition; “Policymaking and the Public, " covering the policymaking process, public opinion, civil society, and populism; and, “Political Economy and Social Policy, " covering industrial, energy, social welfare, agricultural, monetary, and immigration policies, as well as social inequality. In the international relations part, there are four sections: “International Relations Frameworks, " covering grand strategy, international organizations, and international status; “International Political Economy, " covering trade, finance, foreign direct investment, the environment, economic regionalism, and the linkage between security and economics; “International Security, " covering remilitarization, global and regional security multilateralism, nuclear nonproliferation, naval power, space security, and cybersecurity; and, “Foreign Relations” covering Japan’s relations with the United States, China, South Korea, ASEAN, India, the European Union, and Russia. © Oxford University Press 2022. Title: Geopolitics, Geography and Strategy
Affiliations: University of Hull, United Kingdom; Department of Strategic Studies and International Affairs, Britannia Royal Naval College, Dartmouth, United States
Authors with affiliations: Gray C.S., University of Hull, United Kingdom; Sloan G., Department of Strategic Studies and International Affairs, Britannia Royal Naval College, Dartmouth, United States
Abstract: Geopolitical conditions influence all strategic behaviour - even when cooperation among different kinds of military power is expected as the norm, action has to be planned and executed in specific physical environments. The geographical world cannot be avoided, and it happens to be 'organized' into land, sea, air and space - and possibly the electromagnetic spectrum including 'cyberspace'. Although the meaning of geography for strategy is a perpetual historical theme, explicit theory on the subject is only one hundred years old. Ideas about the implication of geographical, especially spatial, relationships for political power - which is to say 'geopolitics'- flourished early in the twentieth century. Divided into theory and practice sections, this volume covers the big names such as Mackinder, Mahan and Haushofer, as well as looking back at the vital influence of weather and geography on naval power in the long age of sail (sixteenth to nineteenth centuries). It also looks forward to the consequences of the revival of geopolitics in post-Soviet Russia and the new space-based field of "astropolitics". © 1999 Taylor & Francis.

Abstract: Integration of communication networks and Shipboard Microgrids (SHMGs) brings significant benefits in the advanced control, monitoring, and remote diagnostics, particularly facilitating the data exchange between various generation components, such as sustainable energy resources, energy storage systems, and connected loads. However, the utilization of communication technologies brings serious cyber-security challenges that highly threaten maritime power systems from a security and stability perspective. This paper aims to present a comprehensive review of cybersecurity issues in marine power systems. Vulnerable points of the system to cyber-attacks, such as phasor measurement units and area control error channels are elaborated. Prevalent attacks in the load frequency control, such as denial of service and false data injection, covert attacks, and reply attacks are discussed. Recent detection/mitigation mechanisms in the cybersecurity field to tackle various cyber-attacks have been introduced. In the detection part, various observers, such as the Kalman filter, Luenberger observer, and machine learning algorithms are studied. In the mitigation mechanism, various methodologies, such as active disturbance rejection control and model predictive control are presented. This survey reviews the recent cyber-security developments and challenges in SHMG, and it is helpful for contemporary researchers in the field of cybersecurity in maritime power systems. © 2025 The Author(s)

Title: Foreign policy of middle powers

Authors with affiliations: Giacomello G., Department of Political and Social Sciences, University of Bologna, Italy; Verbeek B., Department of Political Science, Radboud University Nijmegen, Netherlands
Abstract: Changes in the international political system have given more opportunities for states to seek a more prominent role as a middle power. The contestation of American hegemony and the fragile relations between China, India, and the United States present an external environment that invites states to reconsider their positions. Changes in the nature of power in international politics, both in hard and soft power, have made it possible for some states to seek specific forms of middle power status. This contribution argues that such states may pursue a role as an aspiring global power, a regional power, or a niche power. However, because the search for status in international politics originates from (often competing) ideas of national identity and roles and because the achievement of such status depends on its recognition by relevant other states, an understanding of the choices states make regarding the pursuit of middle power status, requires insights from the scholarship of Foreign Policy Analysis. The argument is illustrated with examples from, amongst others, Iran (regional power), Japan (aspiring global power), and the Netherlands (niche power). © Oxford University Press 2024. Abstract: —The integration of diverse distributed energy resources is increasingly being enabled by shipboard microgrids (SbμGSs) as a promising solution to address the challenges posed by evolving maritime power systems toward decentralized and sustainable architectures. Open communication networks have been recently integrated with sustainable energy resources (SERs) for secure operation, regulation, and management of modern maritime power systems. However, deploying such emerging technologies introduces some faults and delays in communication channels which degrades the performance of marine power systems. This paper focuses on the development of a robust maritime controller-based nonlinear integral-backstepping (NI-BSC) for frequency stabilization of SbμGSs with high penetration of SERs, non-sensitive loads, and battery systems. Particularly, the double deep Q-learning (DDQL) is developed to adaptively design the NI-BSC and dynamically respond to the frequency stabilization challenges of SbμGS. By maximizing a long-term reinforcement signal, the neural networks (NNs) of DDQL (i.e., evaluation and target neural networks) are trained to reduce frequency fluctuations of SbμGS considering communication delays. The considered topology of SbμGS utilizes a separate maritime controller to regulate the solid-oxide fuel cell (SOFC) and thermostatic loads (heat pumps and freezer) while providing the possibility for sustainable units (e.g., wave energy and solar energy) to generate their maximum power. To conduct more realistic examinations, several typical scenarios of shipboard microgrids are carried out in a real-time setup. The real-time simulation outcomes reveal that the controller designed by DDQL outperforms the existing methodologies such as optimal controller, backstepping controller, and model-free sliding mode control, with an improvement in dynamic behaviors ranging from 54.57 % to 74.17 %. © 2025 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Toward a Model-Based Resilience Engineering Framework for Maritime Power Systems
Source title: SysCon 2026 - The 20th Annual IEEE International Systems Conference, Conference Proceedings
Affiliations: Florida State University, Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering, Panama City, United States
Authors with affiliations: Kalantzi C., Florida State University, Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering, Panama City, United States; Gross D.C., Florida State University, Department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering, Panama City, United States
Abstract: Maritime power systems are undergoing a significant transformation driven by the electrification of loads, the increasing demands of high-energy mission systems, and deeper cyber-physical integration. These trends have substantially increased system complexity, which in turn raises the likelihood of faults and failures while complicating degraded-mode operation and graceful failure behavior. As a result, engineers face growing challenges in designing, verifying, and sustaining resilient system behavior under faulted and degraded conditions. It is well established that traditional document-based engineering approaches are insufficient to address these challenges. While model-based systems engineering (MBSE) and its evolution into digital engineering offer promising capabilities, the existing literature provides limited guidance on how these approaches can be systematically applied to engineering resilience in maritime power systems. This paper proposes a resilience-focused MBSE framework, implemented within a digital engineering context, for maritime power systems that supports early reasoning about loss events, recovery strategies, and associated metrics and evidence. The framework establishes explicit, traceable relationships among resilience-related needs, system architecture, recovery behaviors, and verification artifacts, while digital engineering practices enable continuous integration of information across design, simulation, test, and operational domains. By leveraging authoritative models and digital connectivity, the framework supports early identification of vulnerabilities, structured evaluation of recovery strategies, and lifecycle-consistent resilience assessment. The approach is intended to augment existing MBSE practices by making resilience-related assumptions, trade-offs, and evidence explicit, thereby supporting more informed decision-making in the design and sustainment of maritime power systems operating under faulted and degraded conditions.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Navigating New Waters: Homeland Security Challenges in the IMEC Era
Source title: Advances in Science, Technology and Innovation
Affiliations: Rabdan Academy, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
Authors with affiliations: Violakis P., Rabdan Academy, Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates
Abstract: The establishment of the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) aims to promote economic integration amongst India, Europe and the Middle East. However, it also presents significant homeland security challenges. This article assesses the geopolitical implications, specifically focusing on hostilities between Israel and Hamas and maritime aggression by the Houthis. Using a mixed-method approach, the research combines geopolitical theory frameworks—including Mahan’s Sea Power, Mackinder’s Heartland and Spykman’s Rimland theories—with historical case studies and current threat assessments. Findings indicate that ongoing hostilities between Israel and Hamas pose a direct threat to corridor security by disrupting maritime trade, raising insurance costs and destabilising regional cooperation. Simultaneously, Houthi maritime hostility significantly increases risks to critical infrastructure, especially at key chokepoints like Bab El-Mandeb and the Suez Canal. These developments highlight vulnerabilities caused by both state and non-state actors, emphasising the urgent need for multilateral security cooperation amongst IMEC nations. The study recommends policy measures such as joint maritime patrols, strengthening cybersecurity resilience, establishing alternative logistics routes and maintaining ongoing diplomatic efforts. Ultimately, the long-term success of IMEC depends on stakeholders’ ability to collectively address regional threats, protect infrastructure and preserve geopolitical stability. This article provides practical and theoretical insights by highlighting the crucial role of coordinated regional security in protecting economic corridors. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.
